DELIVERABLE: Make provenance a structured contract between stages. (1) The search agent returns JSON findings, each with `claim`, `source_url`, `quote` (verbatim excerpt), `retrieved_at`, and `confidence`; a claim with no source and quote is invalid and is rejected or recorded under `unsupported`, never passed as a finding. (2) A deterministic validator, plain code with no LLM, runs after search: it checks that the schema is complete, that the URL was actually fetched in the agent's tool log, and that the quote appears in the fetched content; failures are dropped or flagged. (3) The writer receives only validated findings and must tag every factual sentence or number with a finding ID (e.g. `[F12]`); statements with no ID must be framed as analysis or opinion, or removed. (4) The editor may change wording but must preserve the ID tags; a post-edit check confirms that every tag still maps to a finding, that every number or percentage in the text appears in its cited quote, and that no untagged factual claims were added. (5) The final report renders tags as citations or a sources section, and any failed check blocks publication and routes the report back for review. Add a regression test using the invented market-share case: a finding with no source must be rejected at the validator, and a report with an untagged figure must fail the final check.

BOUNDARY: Covers the search→writer→editor handoff formats and the deterministic checks between stages, plus the final citation rendering and the regression test. It does not cover judging whether a cited source is itself reliable or correct, changing the search agent's model or prompts beyond the output schema, or the report's design and tone. The quote-match check shows a claim is grounded in a fetched page, not that the page is true. Existing reports already sent to customers are not corrected by this change.

EVIDENCE: Based only on your description of the incident; I have not inspected the repository, so file names, the current agent interfaces, and the tool-log format are unverified, and nothing has been implemented or run. The design should be judged by the regression test above, which reproduces the failure: an unsourced market-share figure must be stopped at the validator, and if it gets past that, the final check must reject any figure that has no tag or a tag whose quote does not contain it.

DELIVERABLE: Do not approve on the 4x ($12,000) assumption yet; the linear-scaling estimate is unreliable and the plan needs a revised model before sign-off. Cost does not scale simply with agent count. Each agent re-reads the same diff and context, so input tokens are multiplied by four. The summary agent also ingests the other three agents' outputs, adding tokens on top. Retries, tool calls, and longer multi-step reasoning in the security and tests agents can push per-agent cost above the single-agent baseline. Shared context could instead be reduced through prompt caching, or by running style on a cheaper model, so the real figure could land either below or above $12,000. Headroom is $3,000 (25%) before the $15,000 limit, which is thin if the summary agent's overhead or per-agent cost growth exceeds roughly 25% in total. Before approval: (1) break the current $3,000 into input tokens, output tokens, and tool calls per review; (2) measure per-agent token usage on a sample of real PRs, not just estimate it; (3) model the summary agent as a function of the three agents' output; (4) calculate a range (best, expected, worst) and confirm the worst case stays under $15,000; (5) add a hard budget cap, per-agent cost alerts, and a rollback plan; (6) consider caching, a cheaper model for style, and skipping agents on trivial PRs.

BOUNDARY: This is a review of the stated assumptions only. I did not edit files, inspect the repository, or see usage data, pricing, the model mix, or PR volume, so I cannot give a corrected dollar figure.
